title: Class pairs whose C. elegans synapse also occurs in Pristionchus pacificus were more co-active in moving C. elegans, but the excess was in global activity modes and unclear under class resampling
abstract: We tested if C. elegans neuron-class pairs whose chemical synapse also occurs in Pristionchus pacificus have higher spontaneous co-activity. Two campaign results found no clear link between this conservation and evoked responses, and named an independent readout as open. We linked undirected class-level anatomy of Cook et al. 2025 (10 C. elegans and 2 P. pacificus maps) and Witvliet 2021 gap junctions to whole-brain calcium imaging of freely moving animals: Atanas et al. 2023 (40 animals, primary) and Dag et al. 2023 (8 animals, replication). Among C. elegans-wired class pairs, pairs with a P. pacificus synapse had higher raw co-activity (+0.46 and +0.50 SD). In the planned model with control for synapse count, presence across 10 maps, gap junctions, contact and class identity, the effect was +0.26 SD (95% class bootstrap -0.11 to 0.78) and +0.16 SD (-0.15 to 0.52); the claim rule was not met. After removal of the first 3 activity principal components, the effect fell to +0.06 and +0.04 SD. Thus conserved synapses join classes that share the global, behaviour-linked modes, without clear extra pair-specific coupling. Gap junctions were detectable (+0.69 SD, 0.03 to 1.69); any chemical synapse was not (+0.10 SD). Limits: class level, 53 classes, no distance control, correlational data.

display.caption: A, B: mean class-pair co-activity (Fisher z) by the number of C. elegans maps with a synapse, with (orange) and without (blue) a P. pacificus synapse; raw (A) and after removal of 3 global modes (B). Filled circles Atanas (40 animals), open squares Dag (8 animals); 95% class bootstrap intervals. C, D: adjusted effects in SD units for controls (grey) and conservation tests (orange).
